title: Running through August 2nd at PAC NYC #musicaltheatre #jennifernettle...
transcript: It's a feminist revenge musical about a woman poisoning a bunch of cruel men, and it's written by and starring Jennifer Nettles. Giulia is inspired by the story of Giulia Tofana, a 17th century Italian apothecary who was suspected of selling poisons to women to murder their husbands. Nettles’s take on this story is simplistic in a lot of ways, but that didn't necessarily bother me. I do think there's a time and a place for a story that's not necessarily trying to be a thoughtful or revelatory reflection on sexism, but instead just offers a cathartic popcorn entertainment fantasy about sticking it to the patriarchy. I don't know that it resonated with me personally the way that it did with some other people in my audience, but that's fine and understandable. And even having said that, I can't deny that I got swept up in the excitement of seeing the downfall of these nasty men and sometimes moved by the moments of tender solidarity among this community of women. When it comes to the music, Jennifer Nettles blends her pop country background with a more musical theatre sound, as well as some rhythm forward musical scenes that feel reminiscent of Hamilton. And there's a propulsive quality to the score that often does pack this dramatic punch and gives the show a rousing sense of spirit. There's also kind of a contemporary edge to the period story, often using modern language in a tongue and cheek way. I do wish They had committed to that lens harder and sooner. It takes a long time for the show to establish a clear sense of tone and focus. There's also like a mysterious narrator figure which feels like a really half-baked and bizarre storytelling device and then just kind of disappears in the second half. So I can't say that this is the tidiest or most thoughtfully rendered story, but actually my biggest gripe with the show was the lyrics more than the book or the music. Some of the more comedic lyrics are more than a little bit cringey, but honestly even that wasn't what I took issue with most cause they kinda deliver it with a playful wink that makes it easy to write off as harmlessly corny. My bigger issue is with the more functional story driven lyrics. So much of it is just the flattest and most obvious declaration of what the character is thinking or feeling in that moment. It's a lot of telling instead of showing. And then a lot of exhausting repetition on top of that. Every line felt like it was part part of a dumbed down Wikipedia summary of the scene you're currently watching. I do really appreciate that Nettles took on the challenge of writing a show that was mostly sung through, where the music feels completely integrated into the storytelling. But I don't think she has, at least right now, the sort of dramaturgical playwriting chops to back that up. So I think this show would have benefited a lot from bringing on another writer.
showTitle: Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo
